note: Phoenix oyster is not named in the textbook or the manual. These notes are the general oyster rules; the drawing is a general oyster form.

stages.a: A colonized block. An X is cut through the bag on its face.
stages.v: Oysters share Pleurotus biology and differ mainly in colour and temperature preference. Blue oysters are opened with side slits or X cuts.

stages.a: Pins push out through the cut.
stages.v: Staple species fruit at 13-18 °C: slower and denser at 13 °C, faster at 18 °C.

stages.a: Fan-shaped caps on longer stems. Their edges still roll under.
stages.v: High CO2 gives long stems and no caps. Watch stem length and cap shape as your airflow gauge.

stages.a: The caps are open, the edges still turned down a little.
stages.v: Oysters are picked before the caps flatten. A good room gives short stems and flattening caps.

stages.a: The caps flatten out and their edges lift.
stages.v: Flat caps mean the pick is past.

stages.a: The edges turn up and split, and the gills shed spores.
stages.v: Spore load matters for staff health.

labels.a: The cut in the bag. The cluster comes out here.
labels.v: Side slits or X cuts, as for blue oyster.

labels.a: A knot of pins at the cut.
labels.v: Blotch shows first on the centre pin of a budding cluster, and on aborted pins at its base.

labels.a: Stems run off-centre into the caps, joined at the base.
labels.v: Short stems mean good airflow; long stems and small caps mean high CO2.

labels.a: A young cap keeps its edge rolled under.
A fan-shaped cap, streaked out from the stem.
Gills run down from the cap onto the stem.
The cap opens flat and its edge lifts.
The edge curls up and splits as the cap ages.
Spores drift down from the gills.
labels.v: Spore load matters for staff health.
